Case study, concept project

TRAVL

A concept 75% mechanical keyboard, sold through one long scroll built around a single number: 4.0 millimeters of travel.

Role
Brand, art direction, interaction design and front-end build
Deliverables
Brand system, scroll-driven product page, colorway configurator
Built with
HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Web Audio; footage generated with Kling
Year
2026
Scroll the experience Open the configurator

The brief

A keyboard is something you feel, and a screen can’t.

TRAVL is a concept brand I made to practice selling a physical product through motion. The problem is built into the category: what makes a keyboard good is how it feels under your fingers, and a web page can only show and tell.

Most keyboard pages answer with a spec table and a rotating render. I wanted the page itself to produce a sensation, so the visitor does something with their hand, which is scroll, and the page answers in the terms a keyboard would: distance, resistance, a click.

The usual keyboard page

  • Switch names and specs up front
  • A render that spins on its own schedule
  • Features listed, never demonstrated
  • Sound left to the imagination

What TRAVL needed to do

  • Build the whole page around one number
  • Show the mechanism instead of naming it
  • Let the visitor set the pace
  • Make sound something you opt into

The idea

One number, used as the interface.

Every switch has a travel distance: how far the key moves before it bottoms out. TRAVL’s is 4.0 mm, and it registers the press halfway, at 2.0 mm. That is the brand’s one claim, so it became the page’s one control.

A counter in the corner reads real millimeters as you scroll. A gauge beside it marks 0, 2.0 and 4.0, and a short label names the state. At 2.0 mm the counter turns terracotta, and if sound is on, the key clicks.

0.0 mm

Resting

The key is up and nothing has happened yet.

Under 2.0 mm

Pre-travel

The stem is moving, but the contacts haven’t met.

2.0 mm

Registered

The contacts close. The counter turns terracotta.

4.0 mm

Bottomed out

The stem hits the housing and the page gives a small jolt.

The story

Nine chapters in one continuous scroll.

The page is a single scene about 22 screens tall. It opens on the whole board, dives into one key, takes it apart, rebuilds the board around it, and ends on the desk it lives on. Each chapter gets one sentence of copy and the rest is image.

  1. Start with one key.

    The camera dives from the whole board into a single keycap.

  2. Take the keycap off.

    The cap lifts away to show the stem, spring and copper contacts.

  3. Press it.

    Scroll presses the switch while the counter and callouts track it.

  4. One becomes eighty-two.

    The same switch repeats across the plate.

  5. Built key by key.

    Warm PBT keycaps land on their switches.

  6. Machined, not molded.

    CNC aluminum with a polished chamfer where the light catches.

  7. Weighted with brass.

    A brushed brass plate underneath adds heft.

  8. Made for the late hours.

    The room warms up, and sound is offered.

  9. Every millimeter, felt.

    The call to action is a key too.

Color

A palette taken from the product itself.

Everything comes from the board: night black for the desk, charcoal and graphite for the aluminum, a warm off-white for the PBT keycaps, brass for the plate, lamp light for the late hours.

The one accent is called Escape because it is the Esc key. The render has exactly one terracotta keycap, and that color is the only accent in the interface: the counter when a key registers, the dot on the gauge, the call to action. Wherever the page asks for attention, it points back at that key.

The page warms as you scroll. Between the brass plate and the late-hours scene the background drifts from cool charcoal toward warm brown, so the light changes before the copy says it’s evening.

Typography

Two typefaces, split by job.

Montserrat carries the brand: the wordmark, the chapter lines and the copy. DM Mono handles readouts: the counter, the callouts and the state label.

Montserrat 700, tracked +0.035emTRAVLThe wordmark and chapter headlines.
DM Mono 400, tabular figures2.0mmThe counter, callouts and state readout.

Numbers don’t jitter

Tabular figures keep the counter from shifting sideways as digits change.

The small mark is wider

The corner wordmark is set at 14 px and tracked out to +0.34em.

Mono is for readouts

Counters, callouts and labels are mono. Headlines and copy are Montserrat.

Buttons

The call to action is a key.

The button is drawn as a keycap with a 5 px lower edge. When pressed, the edge collapses and the button drops by exactly that much. Pressing the real one also runs the counter from 0 to 4.0 and back in half a second, and fires the click.

0.0mm

Under the hood

Scroll is the playhead.

None of the footage plays. Each clip sits paused on a video element, and scroll position sets its time. The visitor controls speed, can stop halfway through a press, and can scrub back.

clips, about 43 seconds of footage
8
screens of scroll from top to end
≈22
footage before and after re-encoding
29 → 8 MB
audio files; the click is synthesized
0

Weighted, not mechanical

The scroll position is eased toward its target with a frame-rate-independent curve, so motion feels like it has mass. Visitors who prefer reduced motion get the raw position instead.

Seams that line up

The clips were generated separately, so each carries a small correction transform that lines it up with its neighbor. Every cross-fade happens between frames that are already registered.

Encoded for scrubbing

When scroll drives video, every frame is a seek. A keyframe every 8 frames keeps seeking near-instant. Playback encodes often space keyframes seconds apart, which makes scrubbing stutter.

One self-contained file

An earlier build fetched its clips by path, which broke the moment the file left its original host. The page now carries its own footage and decodes it locally, so it runs from any host or straight from disk.

A click made from math

A triangle-wave thump falls from 210 Hz to 68 Hz in 50 ms, with a 30 ms burst of band-passed noise around 2.9 kHz on top. It’s off until the visitor turns it on.

Craft

Details that hold up when the clips don’t.

Posters for every clip. A slow or failed load shows a photograph, never a blank stage.

Reduced motion respected. The entrance animation, parallax and scroll smoothing switch off.

Described for screen readers. A hidden heading explains the product, decorative layers are hidden, and photographs carry alt text.

Built for phones. Safe-area insets for notches, and callouts that shorten below 640 px.

Real controls. The sound toggle and the call to action are a button and a link, with visible focus rings.

Quiet by default. Nothing makes a sound until the visitor asks, and the toggle announces its state.

Reflection

What I’d do next.

TRAVL is a concept, so nothing here has met real visitors yet. First, I’d fix the two contrast misses above. Second, I’d test whether 22 screens of scroll holds attention on a phone, and profile video seeking on mid-range devices, where eight scrubbed clips are the likeliest cost.

Third, I’d swap the synthesized click for a recording of a real switch and offer two or three sound profiles, then build the configurator into a full flow from colorway to checkout.
